title: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Within the same continent or area, the extinct forms of the later Tertiary are closely allied to the living inhabitants (e.g. fossil and living marsupials in Australia, edentates in South America), because each area's inhabitants leave modified descendants there.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the great law of the long enduring, but not immutable, succession of the same types within the same areas, is at once explained; for the inhabitants of each quarter of the world will obviously tend to leave in that quarter, during the next succeeding period of time, closely allied though in some degree modified descendants.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On the succession of the same types within the same areas”. Scope: terrestrial mammals, birds and molluscs of continents and islands in the later Tertiary

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-18: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fossil and modern occurrence data permit explicit same-region versus elsewhere comparisons. Phylogenetic harmonization is substantial but feasible for the highlighted vertebrate and molluscan groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For regions with late Tertiary fossils, compare fossil taxa's phylogenetic and morphological proximity to living regional taxa versus living taxa elsewhere. Support requires a significant same-region affinity after controlling for environment and spatial sampling.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Continental boundaries and ranges shifted through time.

Extinction and dispersal can erase local descendants.

fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.67
data existence: 0.91
analysis feasibility: 0.72
operationalizability: 0.88
data adequacy: 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Regional fossil lists and living distributions are both public, and phylogenetic relatedness separates local succession from climatic convergence. Mammals in the later Tertiary are well enough covered for a direct test; birds and molluscs are spottier. The comparison is a standard biogeographic analysis on existing downloads.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For late Cenozoic mammals, birds, and molluscs, compare the relatedness of each region's fossils to that region's living fauna and to the living faunas of other regions. Fossils systematically closest to the local living biota would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Later dispersal and extinction can erase an older regional succession.

Similar climates can produce convergent resemblance that has to be separated with phylogenetic affinity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.7
data existence: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.85

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If each area's later-Tertiary inhabitants left modified descendants in the same area, then the families of terrestrial mammals recorded as fossils on a continent in the Miocene-Pliocene should have living members on that same continent more often than they have living members on any other continent.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Miocene-Pliocene mammal occurrences were downloaded from PBDB for each continent and reduced to families (and genera) with >= 2 occurrences, excluding marine orders and families. Living families (and genera) per continent were taken from GBIF family/genus occurrence facets (>= 20 non-fossil, non-captive records). For each continent the fraction of its fossil families living there today (S) was compared with the mean fraction living on each other continent (O), and the sum of S was compared with all 120 reassignments of living-family sets to continents.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Fossil side: PBDB Miocene-Pliocene (23.03-2.58 Ma) occurrences of Mammalia on each of five continents (Africa, Eurasia = PBDB EUR+ASI, North America, South America, Australia), excluding marine orders/families (Cetacea, Sirenia, Desmostylia, Phocidae, Otariidae, Odobenidae), giving for each continent the set of fossil families with >= 2 occurrences there. Living side: GBIF non-fossil, non-captive occurrence facets by family for Mammalia on each GBIF continent (Europe+Asia merged), a family counting as living on a continent if it has >= 20 such records there (same marine exclusions). For each continent X, S(X) = fraction of X's fossil families that are living on X, and O(X) = mean over the other four continents Y of the fraction of X's fossil families living on Y. Pass if S(X) > O(X) for all five continents AND the pooled ratio mean S / mean O >= 1.2 AND, in a permutation test that randomly reassigns the five living-family sets to continents (all 120 permutations, i.e. exact), the observed sum of S(X) is the maximum or tied maximum (p <= 1/120 + ties). The same statistics at genus level (fossil genera that are extant and living on the same continent) are reported as an extra and do not enter the verdict.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Fails if fossil families are no more likely to survive on their own continent than elsewhere: S(X) <= O(X) for two or more continents, or the pooled ratio is < 1.2, or the observed sum of S(X) is not the maximum over the 120 continent-label permutations. One continent failing with the other conditions met gives 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: ratio of mean same-continent survival fraction to mean other-continent survival fraction, later-Tertiary mammal families

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exact permutation p = 0.0083 (1 of 120 label permutations >= observed)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'closely allied' is read as membership in the same family (his examples, marsupials and edentates, are order- or family-level alliances, so family is a conservative choice). 'Later Tertiary' is read as Miocene plus Pliocene. 'Same continent or area' uses modern continents, merging Europe and Asia. Birds and molluscs, also in the stated scope, are not tested because their later-Tertiary fossil record in PBDB is far sparser and their family-level taxonomy less stable; islands are not tested. The GBIF side measures where families live today, which includes recent introductions (e.g. Muridae everywhere), a bias toward sharing with other continents that works against the claim.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Paleobiology Database Mammalia occurrences, Miocene-Pliocene, genus-resolved, per continent (AFR, EUR, ASI, NOA, SOA, AUS)

GBIF occurrence search API, Mammalia, family and genus facets per continent (non-fossil, non-captive records)

GBIF Backbone Taxonomy species API (names, ranks and orders for family and genus keys)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Family-level alliance is coarse; cosmopolitan families (Bovidae, Felidae, Canidae, Muridae) raise both same- and other-continent fractions and dilute the signal, while endemic families (marsupial and xenarthran families) carry it, as in Darwin's own examples.

GBIF 'living on a continent' includes introduced and feral species (e.g. Muridae and Leporidae in Australia), which biases toward sharing with other continents and so against the claim.

PBDB family assignments and GBIF backbone family names are mostly but not entirely harmonised; mismatched spellings or re-ranked families count as 'not living', equally on all continents.

The Great American Biotic Interchange (c. 3 Ma) means part of South America's Pliocene fauna is of North American origin, which Darwin could not know; it makes the North/South America comparison conservative.

Birds, molluscs and islands, also in the claim's scope, were not tested.
